notes.body:
Two different things love does. The obligatory acts (فرائض) are the ground everyone must stand on — the debt of worship owed, the floor beneath the whole relationship. **They are the most beloved because they are commanded**, and to answer a command is the first proof that a servant belongs to the One who gave it.

But a debt, once paid, asks nothing more. When we go past what was required — praying in the dead of night when no one has asked us to, giving of our vital energy freely — we are no longer discharging a duty; we are making a gift. The voluntary acts (نوافل) matter *precisely because nothing compels them*, and so can come only from the heart. **A freely chosen offering is the one thing that reveals love rather than mere obedience.**

Picture two people. One always pays what he owes on time — reliable, upright, and the relationship holds. Another does that too, and then stays an extra hour, leaves a note no one asked for, gives what was never required. It is the second gesture, owed to no one, that draws the answer "I love him." **Love answers the gift, not the payment.**

That is why the perceiving comes chiefly through the voluntary. The obligatory brings us near and keeps us in good standing; the endless, freely offered surplus is what continues "until I love him," and out of that returned love Allah becomes the servant's hearing and sight. **The obligatory is the doorway; the voluntary is the walking through it, and it has no end.**

And because the voluntary can always be increased — taken further, intensified, drawn to the limits of our strength — it is where the whole self is poured out and gathered into one. This is the drawing near (تقرّب) the chapter turns on, and its inner condition is sincerity (إخلاص): giving not because we must, but because we have given ourselves entirely.
notes.anchor: but it is chiefly through the latter that the slave comes to perceive…
notes.quote: but it is chiefly through the latter that the slave comes to perceive and act through the divine
etymology: فرائض (obligatory acts): from the root ف-ر-ض, to notch, fix, or apportion. A single فريضة is something marked out and fixed in place — a precise, unchangeable allotment. The obligatory duties carry this sense of an amount set by command, a measure that cannot be adjusted.

نوافل (voluntary acts): from the root ن-ف-ل, meaning surplus, an extra portion, even a gift or spoil. A single نافلة is what is added over and above the required minimum — devotion offered beyond the fixed measure, which is exactly why it signals love rather than duty.

تقرّب (drawing near): from the root ق-ر-ب, nearness or closeness. The form here is reflexive and effortful — not simply being near, but actively seeking to close the distance oneself, step by step, which is why the chapter ties it to sustained, strenuous striving.

إخلاص (sincerity): from the root خ-ل-ص, to become pure, clear, and unmixed. To purify a thing is to strip everything foreign out of it, leaving one substance only; sincerity is thus a devotion made single, with no rival motive blended in.

notes.body:
Dhilib al-Yamani was a questioner from Yemen, remembered for the sharp, almost daring manner in which he pressed those he questioned. He came before Maulana Ali — by most accounts during the years of his rule, in the gatherings of Kufa — and asked something that lands like a challenge: had he ever actually seen the One he worshipped? **The daring of the question is exactly the point**, for it is the same posture Glaucon takes toward Socrates, demanding that the highest thing be shown plainly or else confessed unknown.

Maulana Ali's first answer overturns the trap folded inside the question. He would never, he said, worship a Lord he had not seen — so, in a truer sense, he had indeed seen Him. When Dhilib pressed on, asking how such seeing could be, came the reply this book returns to again and again:

لَا تُدْرِكُهُ الْعُيُونُ بِمُشَاهَدَةِ الْعِيَانِ، وَلَٰكِنْ تُدْرِكُهُ الْقُلُوبُ بِحَقَائِقِ الْإِيمَانِ
Eyes see Him not through sight's observation, but hearts see Him through the verities of faith.

The line is drawn between two kinds of seeing. Physical eyes catch only bodies, colours and edges; they can never reach the One who has no likeness and no limit. But the **heart** — the inmost point of our awareness — carries its own sight, opened not by the eye's nerve but by the realities of faith. Where Socrates confessed the Good was beyond his power to describe, Maulana Ali answers out of lived vision rather than argument.

The exchange is preserved among the earliest gathered sayings of Maulana Ali on divine oneness, set in his caliphate at Kufa. **Questioners like Dhilib appear in this record for a reason**: their demand for proof becomes the doorway through which the answer turns us from the outward eye toward a deeper faculty that faith alone awakens.
notes.anchor: Dhilib al-Yamani provocatively asked Ali (ع) whether he had seen
notes.quote: Dhilib al-Yamani provocatively asked Ali (ع) whether he had seen
etymology: ذِعْلِب: a personal name whose root ذ-ع-ل-ب gives ذِعْلِبة, a swift she-camel or ostrich — the underlying sense is darting speed and lightness, an apt echo for a man remembered for quick, probing questions.

يَمَانِي (the Yemeni): from يَمَن (Yemen), itself tied to يَمِين, the right hand and the right side. In Arabic the right carries blessing and good omen, so the land and its people are named from the side of good fortune.

إِيمَان (faith): from the root أ-م-ن, meaning safety and security — the same root as أَمَان (safety) and أَمَانَة (trust). Faith is the heart coming to rest and finding security in what it trusts, not merely assenting to it.
تَوْحِيد (making one): from the root و-ح-د, oneness. The form-II verb وَحَّدَ means to make many into one, so تَوْحِيد is the act of both declaring and inwardly realizing that Allah is utterly one.

notes.body:
The whole claim turns on one word, إحسان — worshipping Allah as though we behold Him, even while knowing that if we cannot see Him, He surely sees us. When the passage speaks of the currents "most hostile to the mystical tradition," it means **those movements that reject this inward dimension of faith**, the contemplative or Sufi current; the text names them by that hostility rather than by any particular sect.

The basis for the claim is not a headcount of who did what, but a diagnosis of what religion becomes once its inner life is removed. Stripped of إحسان, faith hardens into an **outer shell** — an ideology driven by individual passion and open to political manipulation. A shell can be pointed at anything.

The causal thread runs through the heart. A virtue cut off from its divine root becomes **situational and self-serving**, bending the moment circumstances change. The remembrance of Allah, ذكر, is what keeps each thing in its proper place, including the ego, which is effaced in prostration. Remove that discipline, and the ego is left sovereign, until a person can imagine harming creation in order to please its Creator — the very contradiction that إحسان makes unthinkable.

Seen this way, إحسان holds together three things that violence tears apart:

- devotion to Allah and kindness toward His creation, which cannot be separated;
- the inner intention and the outer act, bound into one;
- the self and its Lord, so that the ego never becomes its own final authority.

So the link is offered as **spiritual logic, not statistics**: those furthest from this polishing of the heart are the likeliest to reduce a whole religion to a weapon.
notes.anchor: those most prone to terrorism in the name of Islam have emerged from…
notes.quote: those most prone to terrorism in the name of Islam have emerged from the currents most hostile to the ihsani
etymology: إحسان (excellence, beautiful doing): from the root ح-س-ن, to be beautiful or good. To perform إحسان is to make an action beautiful from within — here, to worship Allah as if beholding Him, giving the deed its inward quality and not merely its outward form.

ذكر (remembrance): from the root ذ-ك-ر, to recall or to mention. It is at once the tongue's naming of a divine Name and the heart's constant awareness — a polishing that lets the heart see after blindness and hear after deafness.

تقرب (drawing near): from the root ق-ر-ب, nearness or closeness. The form carries the sense of effort toward closeness — the soul actively approaching Allah through devotion, so that nearness is won rather than merely wished for.
